id: Daily Trials by a Sensitive Man

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Oh, there are times When all this fret and tumult that we hear Do seem more stale than to the sexton’s ear His own dull chimes. Ding dong! ding dong! The world is in a simmer like a sea Over a pent volcano,—woe is me All the day long! From crib to shroud! Nurse o’er our cradles screameth lullaby, And friends in boots tramp round us as we die, Snuffling aloud. At morning’s call The small-voiced pug-dog welcomes in the sun, And flea-bit mongrels, wakening one by one, Give answer all. When evening dim Draws round us, then the lonely caterwaul, Tart solo, sour duet, and general squall,— These are our hymn. Women, with tongues Like polar needles, ever on the jar; Men, plugless word-spouts, whose deep fountains are Within their lungs. Children, with drums Strapped round them by the fond paternal ass; Peripatetics with a blade of grass Between their thumbs. Vagrants, whose arts Have caged some devil in their mad machine, Which grinding, squeaks, with husky groans between, Come out by starts. Cockneys that kill Thin horses of a Sunday,—men, with clams, Hoarse as young bisons roaring for their dams From hill to hill. Soldiers, with guns, Making a nuisance of the blessed air, Child-crying bellman, children in despair, Screeching for buns. Storms, thunders, waves! Howl, crash, and bellow till ye get your fill; Ye sometimes rest; men never can be still But in their graves.

Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

This poem, by Oliver Wendell Holmes, satirically catalogs the relentless cacophony of everyday human existence—from cradle to grave—using vivid imagery of screaming nurses, chattering women, blustering men, barking dogs, and street noise to depict life as an unending torrent of clamor.

outputs.L1:
Oh, there are times
When all this fret and tumult that we hear
Do seem more stale than to the sexton's ear
His own dull chimes.

Ding dong! ding dong!
The world is in a simmer like a sea
Above a pent-up volcano,—woe is me
All the day long!

From crib to shroud!
The nurse above our cradles screams her lullaby,
And friends in boots come tramping as we die,
Snuffling aloud.

At morning's call
The small-voiced pug-dog welcomes in the sun,
And flea-bit mongrels, wakening one by one,
Give answer all.

When evening dim
Draws close around us, then the lone caterwaul,
Tart solo, sour duet, and general squall,—
These are our hymn.

Women, with tongues
Like polar needles, ever on the jar;
Men, plugless word-spouts, whose deep fountains are
Within their lungs.

Children, with drums
Strapped round them by the fond paternal ass;
Peripatetics with a blade of grass
Between their thumbs.

Vagrants, whose arts
Have caged some devil in their maddened machine,
Which, grinding, squeaks, with husky groans between,
Come out by starts.

Cockneys that kill
Thin horses of a Sunday,—men, with clams,
Hoarse as young bisons roaring for their dams
From hill to hill.

Soldiers, with guns,
Making a nuisance of the blessed air,
Child-crying bellman, children in despair,
Screeching for buns.

Storms, thunders, waves!
Howl, crash, and bellow till ye have your fill;
Ye sometimes rest; but men can ne'er be still

outputs.L2:
There are moments when every bit of this noisy commotion we listen to feels even more tiresome to us than the monotonous ringing of his own bells sounds to the gravedigger. Ding dong! ding dong! The whole world bubbles and churns like an ocean sitting atop a bottled-up volcano—how miserable I am the entire day through!

From the moment we're born until we're buried! A nurse shrieks lullabies above our infant beds, and later, companions wearing boots stomp about us while we lie dying, sniffling noisily.

When morning summons us, the yappy little pug-dog greets the rising sun, and flea-ridden mutts, stirring from sleep one after another, all bark in reply.

As the dusk gathers dimly around us, then comes the solitary cat's wailing, the sharp solo, the bitter duet, and the widespread shrieking—such is the song we're given.

Women whose tongues point steadily like compass needles, forever quarreling; men who are like unstoppable spouts of speech, with their bottomless sources buried deep inside their chests.

Children carrying drums that some doting foolish father has strapped onto them; wanderers strolling along while whistling through a blade of grass held between their thumbs.

Drifters whose skill has trapped some demon inside their crazy contraption, which, as it turns, squeals and lets out rough moans in fits and bursts.

City dwellers who work thin horses to death on Sundays—men bellowing through shells, as hoarse as baby buffaloes crying out for their mothers across the hills.

Soldiers with rifles, spoiling the sweet air; a bellman who makes children weep, and children in misery, screaming for their buns.

Storms, thunderclaps, and waves! Go ahead and howl, crash, and roar until you're satisfied—yet you at least fall quiet now and then. People, though, can only find stillness once they're in their graves.
outputs.L3:
# The Weariness of Constant Noise

I am weary, worn down to the very bone by the ceaseless noise and turmoil that pervades every moment of our daily existence. There seems to be no escape from it, no quiet corner in which the soul might find a moment's rest. The clamor presses upon me from all sides, relentless and unforgiving, until I feel utterly overwhelmed by the sheer weight of it.

Consider how human life is saturated with sound from its very beginning to its final end. We enter the world accompanied by noise, and we depart in the same manner. Even the nurse, who ought to soothe and comfort, seems to scream her lullabies rather than sing them, while around the bed of the dying, mourners tramp and shuffle, filling what should be a solemn silence with their restless movement. From the cradle to the grave, we are denied true quiet.

Nor does the natural world offer any refuge from this endless din. At the break of morning, dogs begin their barking, shattering the peace of dawn. And when evening comes, bringing with it the promise of rest, we hear instead the caterwauling of cats and the squalling of countless creatures. The animals contribute their own voices to the great chorus of noise that surrounds us at every hour.

People of every kind add their share to this ceaseless clamor. Loud women raise their voices in argument or gossip; talkative men prattle on without pause; children beat upon their drums with tireless energy. Vagrants call out in the streets, and soldiers screech and shout as they go about their business. Whatever direction one turns, there is another voice, another sound, another disturbance to trouble the weary spirit.

It strikes me that even the most violent storms, for all their fury, must eventually spend themselves and fall quiet. The tempest rages, but in time it passes and grows still. For human beings, however, there is no such respite. We alone are denied this natural rest, and can find true silence and lasting peace only in death itself. Until that final hour arrives, we must endure the endless noise of living.
outputs.L4:
# On the Perpetual Noise of Human Existence

Oliver Wendell Holmes offers us, in this wry and observant poem, a satirical inventory of the ceaseless clamor that accompanies human life at every stage. From the very moment of our entrance into the world, we are surrounded by sound. The poem opens, fittingly, at the cradle, where the newborn's arrival is heralded not by peace but by the screaming of nurses—an ironic welcome that establishes the theme at once. Life begins in noise, and, as Holmes will demonstrate, it continues that way to the very end.

With a gentle but pointed humor, the poem catalogs the various sources of this relentless cacophony. There are the women chattering endlessly, their voices weaving an unbroken thread of conversation through the fabric of daily life. There are the men blustering with self-importance, filling the air with the sounds of their opinions and their quarrels. Beyond the human voices lie the animal ones: dogs barking in the streets, adding their own contribution to the din. And enveloping all of this is the general noise of the street itself—the rumble of traffic, the cries of vendors, the countless small commotions that make up the soundscape of a living town. Holmes assembles these images with an accumulating force, so that the reader begins to feel the exhausting weight of it all, the sense of a world that never once pauses to draw a quiet breath.

The genius of the poem lies in its turn, delivered in the closing lines. Holmes reminds us that even nature, in her most violent moods, eventually grows still. The storms that rage across the sky spend themselves and pass; the thunders that shake the heavens roll away into silence. There is, in the natural world, a rhythm of tumult and repose, of clamor followed by calm. But humanity, the poem observes, enjoys no such reprieve. The noise of human living admits no interval, no natural rest. For us, true stillness comes only in death—the single, final silence that our restless species can attain.

This is the source of the poem's wry, melancholy wit. What might have been a simple complaint about a noisy world becomes, through Holmes's closing insight, a broader meditation on the human condition. To be alive, the poem suggests with a knowing smile, is to be perpetually in the midst of sound and commotion; peace and quiet are not the natural companions of existence but its rare exception, purchased only at the ultimate price. In cataloging the clamor of life from cradle to grave, Holmes gently mocks our incessant human busyness even as he acknowledges the strange truth beneath the joke: that the only lasting stillness we may ever know is the one that awaits us all.
outputs.L5:
# The Sound of Ding

When the old grandfather clock struck midnight, a familiar **ding** echoed through the silent house. It was a sound that had marked the passing of time for three generations, and no one in the family could imagine the home without it.

**His** name was Thomas, and he had inherited the clock from his father, who had received it from his own father before him. The clock stood proudly in the hallway, its polished wood gleaming under the soft light of the chandelier. Every hour, without fail, it would announce the time with that distinctive **ding** that everyone had grown to love.

**When** Thomas was a young boy, he would sit at the bottom of the stairs, waiting eagerly for the clock to chime. **His** favorite moment was midnight, when the twelve chimes seemed to last forever. Each **ding** felt magical, as if the clock were casting a spell over the household, wrapping everyone in a blanket of comfort and tradition.

Years passed, and **his** children grew up hearing the same reassuring sound. **When** they moved away to start their own lives, they often spoke of how much they missed that gentle **ding** that had defined their childhood evenings.

Now, as an old man himself, Thomas still smiled **when** he heard the clock chime. **His** heart filled with warmth, knowing that this simple sound connected him to the past and, hopefully, to the future. **When** his grandchildren visited, they too would pause and listen, mesmerized by the same **ding** that had captivated their grandfather so many years ago.

Some things, Thomas thought, were meant to last forever.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a humorous poem complaining about all the noises of daily life, from morning dogs to evening cats to loud people, using short four-line stanzas with a very short final line in each.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Symphony of Suffering

At dawn the neighbor's dog awakes,
He barks at every leaf that shakes,
He howls at shadows, birds, and breeze,
Oh please.

The garbage truck arrives at seven,
Its crashing sounds ascend to heaven,
It beeps and grinds with metal groans,
My bones.

The coffee shop's espresso hiss,
The whistling kettle's angry kiss,
A blender screams its morning song,
So wrong.

By noon the construction crew appears,
With jackhammers to pierce my ears,
They drill and pound the livelong day,
I pray.

The office phones all ring at once,
My cubicle mate loudly grunts,
He chews his gum with mouth ajar,
You star.

The lady on the train recites
Her weekend plans and legal fights,
Her phone on speaker, volume high,
Oh why.

At last I'm home, I close the door,
But now the upstairs kids explore,
They gallop like a herd of deer,
Right here.

And then the evening cats convene,
The loudest opera ever seen,
They yowl of love beneath the moon,
Too soon.

I lie in bed and shut my eyes,
The silence feels like sweet surprise,
Then somewhere far a car alarm—
Disarm!
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a satirical Victorian-style poem about how the world is full of endless noise and clamor, and only in death do we find true silence.
counterfactuals.output:
**On the Solace of the Sepulchre**

Behold this world, a raucous, ceaseless din,
Where church-bells clang and costermongers bawl,
Where omnibus and organ-grinder's tin
Conspire to leave no peace to man at all.

The infant shrieks, the fishwife hawks her wares,
The parson thunders threats of endless flame,
The neighbour's parrot damns you unawares,
And gossips buzz to sully your good name.

The railway whistles pierce the morning fog,
The dogs pursue the cats with mad halloo,
Your mother-in-law, a most incessant cog,
Grinds out her grievances the whole day through.

Society's a most exhausting rout—
The waltz, the ball, the tedious dinner-hour,
Where wits contend to speak, but not to doubt,
And silence is a flower none dares to flower.

Yet weep not, gentle sufferer of the age,
For Providence has fixed a sure retreat:
No creditor may there presume to rage,
Nor may the milkman thunder in the street.

'Tis not in monastery, spa, or nook,
Nor cotton stuffed devoutly in the ear,
Nor in the pages of a soothing book—
But six feet down, dear reader, calm is here!

The tomb! O blessed dormitory deep,
Where no alarm-clock rends the tranquil breast,
Where one may take at last a proper sleep,
And even the worms observe their guest's request.

So when your nerves are frayed and life is loud,
Take comfort in this cheering, cheerful truth:
The quietest of parlours is a shroud—
And Death's the only tenant of the booth!

Then let the trumpets bray and cymbals crash,
Let all creation caterwaul and roar;
We'll bear it, knowing that, when we're but ash,
We shall not hear the wretched thing once more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write me a comic verse in the style of Oliver Wendell Holmes about the ceaseless racket humans make throughout life?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Perpetual Din**

From that first squall in which we all begin,
Man enters life by making such a din!
The nursery rings with tyrant infant cries—
No throne so loud, no despot half his size;
He rules the household from his flannel state
And bellows till the very cradles quake.

Then comes the schoolboy, whooping down the stair,
Whose lungs could fright a lion from his lair;
He shouts at marbles, hollers at his hoops,
And splits the welkin with his gleeful whoops.
No hurricane that ever swept the coast
Could match one lad who's caught a cricket-post.

The youth grows up—and, gracious, how he talks!
He argues, orates, whistles as he walks;
He courts his lady in a serenade
That routs the neighbors and appalls the maid;
He weds—and lo, the church-bells clang and swing,
As though creation cracked to hear him ring.

In manhood's prime he thunders at the bar,
Or drums the pulpit, audible afar;
He pounds the table, roars across the town,
And beats his rivals verbally to ground.
The clatter of his commerce fills the street—
A symphony of tongues and trampling feet.

Old age arrives; you'd think at last he'd cease—
But no! He grumbles louder for his peace!
He coughs, he creaks, he lectures every guest,
And snores like Etna when he seeks his rest.
Yea, to the grave he goes with clamor still,
For then the mourners weep against their will,

And after all his years of noise and breath,
A stone must *speak* his silence into death!
So here lies Man, at last serene and mute—
The only quiet thing about the brute.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poem titled "The Music-Grinders" that lists all the annoying sounds a person endures from birth to death.
counterfactuals.output:
I should note that there's a real poem called "The Music-Grinders" by Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. (1830s), but it's actually a satire about street organ-grinders demanding money—not quite a catalog of life's annoying sounds. Since I can't reliably reproduce its exact original text from memory, here's an **original** poem I've written to match the theme you describe:

---

**The Music-Grinders**

We enter to a wailing note,
the first cry from our throat,
then slam of doors, the rattled crib,
the spoon against the bib.

The playground shriek, the whistle's blast,
the school bell tolling fast,
the scrape of chalk, the ruler's crack,
the taunts behind our back.

The dripping tap that will not cease,
the neighbor's midnight feast,
the barking dog, the car alarm,
the drone of false alarm.

The office hum, the printer's groan,
the buzzing of the phone,
the meeting's murmur, chairman's cough,
the clock that ticks time off.

The traffic's grind, the sirens' moan,
the jackhammer on stone,
the toddler's tantrum, kettle's scream,
the interrupted dream.

The waiting-room's forgotten tune,
the buzzing fluorescent noon,
the hollow tick of hospice halls,
the whispered word that falls—

And last of all, a bell's slow toll
to grind us to the goal;
we leave as loudly as we came,
still deaf to our own name.

---

Would you like me to adjust the tone (more comic, more somber), or shorten it? And if you specifically wanted the *original* Holmes poem, I can point you toward reliable sources for its full text.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a witty poem with an irregular rhyme scheme cataloging noisy nuisances—barking dogs, chattering women, blustering men, drumming children, street organ players—ending with the idea that people are never still except in the grave.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Perpetual Racket**

The dogs are at it, one and all,
A choir of barks from wall to wall—
One yaps at leaves, one bays the moon,
One howls off-key a broken tune,
And when at last they cease to bark,
Some newer nuisance splits the dark.

For here come women, two, then three,
A cataract of chattery glee,
Their tongues like millwheels never tire—
They gossip, giggle, and conspire,
And should one pause to draw her breath,
Another talks her half to death.

Then men arrive to bluster loud,
Each puffed and pompous, stiff and proud,
They thump the table, roar their views,
Debate the tax, dispute the news,
And swear the world would run first-rate
If only *they* controlled the state.

The children next! O spare my head—
They drum on pots, on pans, on lead,
They bang, they clang, they shriek, they run,
And call this hideous uproar *fun*;
No angel choir could match, I vow,
The din a small boy makes right now.

And through it all, to crown my woe,
The organ-grinder cranks his show,
That wheezing, groaning, tortured air
Repeated, God knows why or where,
Until the very cobbles moan
And beg the fellow to move on.

So round the clock the tumult swells—
The barks, the chats, the boasts, the bells;
I've sought for silence high and low
In every earthly place I know,
And found this truth beyond all doubt:
Man makes his noise till life gives out.

The only hush that's truly deep,
Where neither dog nor drum can creep,
Where women hold their tongues at last
And blustering men are bound and fast—
Is that cold, quiet, welcome shelf
Where each man, still, keeps to himself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
